t: A Privileged Position? The Influence of Business Interests in Government Consultations
abs: The relative influence of business interests in the formulation of public policy is disputed, and empirical results remain inconclusive. Business groups are generally expected to be more successful than other groups in influencing public policy because they are able to deliver detailed and technical knowledge about their sector and because the welfare of business is crucial for the economic well-being of society. However, based on an exchange relation logic we argue that the lobbying resources of business groups are not equally important across policy areas. We study overt influence in one stage in the policy-making process and test how business influence is moderated by policy issue in a dataset containing all consultations on Danish bills in the parliamentary year 2009/10. In consultations regarding business regulation, business groups are indeed more influential than other interest groups; but in consultations regarding public sector services and general regulation, nonbusiness groups tend to be more successful than business groups. Business has a privileged position but only on its home turf.

t: Improving Outcomes in Fiscal Federalism: Local Political Leadership and Administrative Capacity
abs: This study investigates how the political influence of local elected officials and the administrative capacities of local administrative agencies together shape outcomes in fiscal federalism. The results demonstrate that differences in support and direct involvements of local officials in federally funded energy programs influence the timeliness of implementation processes. Direct mayoral involvement in the grant application process increases the likelihood of on-time or early implementation of public projects, but direct city council involvement increases implementation time. On the other hand, general policy support from mayors and council members for these efforts, without direct involvement in program design, made on-time or early implementation of public projects more likely. Este estudo investiga como a influência política de administradores locais eleitos e a capacidade administrativa das agências administrativas locais geram resultados no federalismo fiscal. Os resultados demonstram que diferenças no suporte e envolvimento direto de oficiais locais em programas de energia financiados pelo governo federal influenciam o cronograma dos processos de implementação. O envolvimento direto dos prefeitos no processo de aplicação de recursos aumenta a probabilidade de pontualidade ou mesmo implementação antecipada dos projetos públicos, mas o envolvimento direto da Câmara dos Vereadores aumenta o tempo de implementação. Por outro lado, o apoio político de prefeitos e vereadores para estes esforços, sem envolvimento direto no desenho do programa, aumenta a probabilidade dos projetos serem antecipados ou entregues na data certa. Translated by Ricardo Gomes, University of Brasília

t: Regulatory Compliance when the Rule of Law Is Weak: Evidence from China’s Environmental Reform
abs: What drives regulatees’ behaviors when the institution of law is weak? This study seeks to answer the question by examining environmental regulation enforcement in China. Based on survey and interview data on Hong Kong-owned manufacturing enterprises in the Pearl River Delta Region, Guangdong Province, we found that their decisions to adopt basic and proactive environmental management practices were less driven by concerns for legality than by their perceptions of the regulators’ actions and gestures. Enterprises adopted basic environmental practices to avoid potential punishment and more proactive practices to avoid potentially arbitrary impositions from regulatory officials. Regulated enterprises were more likely to adopt both basic and proactive environmental practices if they had less difficulties in understanding the enforced regulations. These findings suggest important ways in which regulatory compliance behaviors in a developmental context may differ from those in Western countries.

t: Understanding Satisfaction with Schools: The Role of Expectations
abs: Using a nationally representative survey, this article examines how citizen satisfaction with one public institution, public schools, is shaped by normative expectations regarding what goals schools ought to pursue. We expand extant literature on the role of expectations in shaping satisfaction, which typically focuses on performance expectations, by exploring goal expectations. Using a constant sum allocation exercise, we find that individuals typically express one of two distinct preferences for what goals schools ought to pursue—an academic focus versus a well-rounded focus. We then show that individuals holding these different goal expectations express different levels of satisfaction when viewing the same school performance data. Our results suggest that policies disproportionately focusing on a single goal or expectation may alter public satisfaction, which could negatively influence ongoing support.

t: What Do We Talk about When We Talk about "Research"? A Guide to Interpretive Research Talk for Natives and Nonnatives
abs: I love music. There is virtually no genre of it that doesn’t belong in my collection. When I look across that collection, Duke Ellington often comes to mind. Ellington famously said, “There are two kinds of music. Good music, and the other kind.” Having thought now for many years about social research and the politics of categorization, I now hear in Ellington’s comment a prompt to think about how we organize and evaluate things in our world. I wonder, does Ellington mean to do away with all the genres and subgenres of music and for us to put all music into either a “good” or “other” bucket? Or does he mean that we should break apart the two buckets and relish in the proliferation of genres, subgenres, and all the people and places good music comes from? Does that proliferation, then, make the category of “genre” meaningless, thereby returning us to simply “good music” and “the other kind”? For me, the practical upshot of Ellington’s comment is this: We should approach the task of categorization and judgment with circumspection. We would do well to be conscious of the criteria and instruments that we use to judge the good and the other, and to avoid conflating “the good” with a specific kind.

t: Regulation in the American States
abs: Stuart Shapiro and Debra Borie-Holtz have done the scholarly community a service in their new book, The Politics of Regulatory Reform. The book provides some of the first empirical traction on the imposition and effects of regulatory reforms across the 50 American states—a topic that has long been recognized as important but has been infrequently investigated systematically. In part, this topic has escaped close scrutiny because the data necessary to compare across these 50 different governmental units have proved difficult and time consuming to collect. In this book, Shapiro and Borie-Holtz make important inroads toward correcting this deficiency. Put broadly, the “take away” message from Shapiro and Borie-Holtz’s book is that regulatory reforms are frequently passed by American state legislatures, but, on average, the authors conclude that these reforms hold little practical impact. Indeed, the book implies at several points that these reforms should, generally speaking, be seen as symbolic actions taken by elected politicians. State legislators, the book implies, may pass regulatory reforms because they are easier to enact than more intrusive and presumably more effective ways of controlling or directing agency regulatory activities, such as passing specific statues or holding oversight hearings.

t: How (Not) to Solve the Problem: An Evaluation of Scholarly Responses to Common Source Bias
abs: Public administration scholars are beginning to pay more attention to the problem of common source bias, but little is known about the approaches that applied researchers are adopting as they attempt to confront the issue in their own research. In this essay, we consider the various responses taken by the authors of six articles in this journal. We draw attention to important nuances of the common measurement issue that have previously received little attention and run a set of empirical analyses in order to test the effectiveness of several proposed solutions to the common-source-bias problem. Our results indicate that none of the statistical remedies being used by public administration scholars appear to be reliable methods of countering the problem. Currently, it appears as though the only reliable solution is to find independent sources of data when perceptual survey measures are employed.

t: Explaining Coordination in Collaborative Partnerships and Clarifying the Scope of the Belief Homophily Hypothesis
abs: The move towards collaborative governance in environmental policy often takes the form of collaborative partnerships involving multiple stakeholders with divergent beliefs and interests. Within such partnerships, stakeholders selectively coordinate with one another to varying degrees to achieve both individual and shared objectives. Using interview and questionnaire data from 10 US marine aquaculture partnerships in 2009–2011, we test three theoretical hypotheses regarding how individuals within collaborative partnerships decide with whom to coordinate. These competing propositions include belief homophily (individuals will coordinate with whom they share beliefs), trust (individuals will coordinate with those whom they trust), and resources (individuals will coordinate with those who hold critical resources). Results suggest that specific aspects of trust and resources are more important than shared beliefs in driving coordination in marine aquaculture partnerships. This finding qualifies previous studies that identified shared beliefs as a driving factor. This study concludes with a theoretical discussion about the explanatory boundaries of belief homophily.

t: Personal Attributes and Institutions: Gender and the Behavior of Public Employees. Why Gender Matters to not only “Gendered Policy Areas”
abs: Do men and women carry out the same jobs differently? Based on a unique data set from six different Danish public occupations and building on sociological and neurological gender studies together with institutionalism and studies on individual diversity in street-level bureaucrats’ behavior, the article argues and empirically demonstrates how the gender of public employees affects their behavior, but that the effect is conditioned by the regulative institutions of the specific task. Next, the article shows that the effect is partly explained by differences in personal attributes such as empathy, systemizing, and competitiveness. Through these findings, the article contributes to the studies on representative bureaucracy by showing that gender not only affects bureaucratic behavior based on differences in interests but also on differences in attributes. Scholarly interest in the effects of gender should therefore not be restricted to “gendered policy areas.” Likewise, scholars of public employee behavior should supplement its focus on differences in interests and policy preferences with a focus on differences in personal attributes and abilities. Otherwise, we run the risk of ignoring potential explanations for public employee behavior. Finally, the article contributes to the literature on public administration and management by elucidating the contingent effect of regulative institutions. Existe alguma diferença na forma que homens e mulheres desempenham os mesmos trabalhos? Baseado em uma base de dados única de seis diferentes ocupações públicas dinamarquesas e construído sobre estudos sociológicos e neurológicos de gênero junto com institucionalismo e estudos sobre diversidade individual do comportamento de burocratas de nível de rua, o artigo argumenta e demonstra empiricamente como o gênero dos empregados públicos afeta seu comportamento, mas que o efeito é condicionado por instituições regulatórias de tarefa especifica. Em seguida, o artigo demonstra que o efeito é parcialmente explicado pelas diferenças de atitudes pessoais, tais como empatia, sistematização e competitividade. Através destas descobertas, o artigo contribui para estudos sobre burocracia representativa, demonstrando que o gênero não somente afeta o comportamento burocrático baseado nas diferenças em interesses, mas também nas diferenças em atributos. Interesse acadêmico nos efeitos do gênero não deverá, desta forma, ser restrito à “áreas de políticas de gênero”. Da mesma forma, pesquisadores com interesse em analisar o comportamento de empregados públicos devem complementar o seu foco nas diferenças em interesses e preferências políticas com um foco específico nas diferenças de atributos pessoais e habilidades. Caso contrário, corremos o risco de ignorar explicações potenciais para o comportamento de empregados públicos. Finalmente, o artigo contribui com a literatura em administração pública através da explanação dos efeitos contingentes das instituições regulatórias. Translated by Ricardo Gomes, University of Brasília

t: The Politics of Detection in Business Regulation
abs: Detecting noncompliant behaviors is an important step in the enforcement of regulations. The literature on the subject is vast yet also narrow in its approach, in the sense that it has built on the assumption that regulators would always want to maximize information quantity and quality, while acting under two fundamental constraints: the regulator’s resources and the information asymmetry between regulator and regulatee. This article argues that regulatory agencies might not always want to maximize information: rather, other bureaucratic goals and concerns might shape detection preferences and tools of detection in what might seem to be unexpected and irrational ways. To support this argument, the article presents a case study of the regulation of industrial risks in France, which focuses on the detection of incidents—small losses of control—taking place in high-hazard sites. The study presents a rich set of observations. It finds regulators sharing with regulatees a restrictive interpretation of incident reporting obligations. It identifies also a range of third party informants—employees—who have been neither solicited by regulators to contribute to detecting incidents, nor have been particularly well received by them when they have done so. The motives of regulators that can account for these detection preferences are mixed, but an overarching one appears to be their concerns for reputational risk. Seen through such a lens, certain types of incidents and certain tools for detecting them appeared either unimportant, or on the contrary as deserving attention and effort. On the basis of the case study and other empirical illustrations found in the literature, the article then offers a more general argument about how bureaucratic reputation may shape detection practices in business regulation.

t: Naive Cronyism and Neutral Competence: Patronage, Performance, and Policy Agreement in Executive Appointments
abs: Much of the bureaucratic literature suggests that, when staffing the bureaucracy, executives want agents who are both responsive to their political needs and possess the competence needed to fulfill their directives. However, institutional barriers—such as the requirement for legislative confirmation—exist that may make pursuing a strategy of responsive competence difficult, if not impossible. Here, I examine a model of bureaucratic appointments that allows for informationally imperfect agencies. I show that when legislative assent is required, trade-offs between ideology and either patronage or agency performance—or both—are often required to ensure legislative confirmation. The same dynamics are not present for unilateral appointments. Finally, using a data set that incorporates the ideologies of federal program managers, the performance of federal programs, and whether program managers were patronage appointees, I conduct a series of empirical tests that support the model’s predictions.

t: Developing and Testing a New Goal Taxonomy: Accounting for the Complexity of Ambiguity and Political Support
abs: Scholars have long argued clear organizational goals enhance performance whereas ambiguous goals diminish it. Yet, such arguments often overlook the beneficial aspects of ambiguous goals. Therefore, this study proposes and tests a new goal taxonomy that examines the dynamic, mixed effects of goal ambiguity on employees in public organizations. The taxonomy proposed accounts for varying degrees of goal ambiguity and political support. It also considers how different combinations of political support and goal ambiguity affect employees’ role clarity. Findings from a latent class analysis support the proposed taxonomy and indicate role clarity is at its lowest levels when employees confront unsupportive political bodies and ambiguous goals. However, the level of role clarity employees experience in an organization differs when other combinations of political support and goal ambiguity are considered.

t: Public Values in Public Administration
abs: “Clearly the lack of consensus on public values tempers our ability to develop simple analytical tools.” (Bozeman 2002, 150) The insight that values are at the heart of public administration is not at all new. Dahl, for instance, stated in 1947 that the core questions in public administration concern responsibility, which “hinges ultimately on some definition of ends, purposes and values in society” (p. 3). The recent rise of public value(s) as a core concept is, nonetheless, remarkable. Particularly conducive to this upsurge was Mark Moore’s Creating Public Value (1995), a book applauded as an attempt to pull public management thinking away from its business envy and imbue it with attention to the specific normative traits of the public sector. Moore’s basic idea was to guide the strategic management of public organizations by using the notion of public value “in a similar way to which notions of private value had provided strategic purpose for private sector managers” (Benington and Moore 2011a, 1), so roughly as an equivalent of shareholder value in business. At the center of the project are the two values of efficiency and fairness, indicating that management is not just a technical affair but involves normative ideas as well (Moore 1995, 28).

t: Benchmarking and Interorganizational Learning in Local Government
abs: Scholars have questioned the value of benchmarking as a means of advancing public sector performance and innovation, pointing instead to evidence of isomorphism among benchmarking organizations. The authors of this article assert that different types of bench-marking should be distinguished from one another in such assessments and suggest that the verdict for best practice benchmarking will differ from that for the more common form of benchmarking in the public sector, comparisons of performance statistics. They note that the absence of a coherent theory of public sector benchmarking—one relating benchmark-ing to interorganizational learning—restricts hypothesis formulation and testing and, hence, our understanding of the efficacy of this management practice in its different forms. This article offers five propositions on benchmarking and interorganizational learning, drawn from research literature and the experience of a set of city governments engaged in a best practice benchmarking project, as a step toward developing a theory of public sector benchmarking. t: Altruism by Job Sector: Can Public Sector Employees Lead the Way in Rebuilding Social Capital?
abs: The face of public service continues to evolve as government copes with increasingly complex societal problems and changing means of service delivery. Public managers are now challenged to oversee programs that cut across sectors and organizational boundaries, and people carrying out the government’s work can be found across all sectors—government, nonprofit, and for-profit. Unlike those in previous generations, younger individuals see opportunities to engage in public service in nonprofit and for-profit organizations, which has undoubtedly affected the ability of government agencies to recruit and retain those with public service values. Have opportunities to engage in public service across sectors made differences between public, nonprofit, and for-profit organizations irrelevant? Are public and nonprofit employees any different from those in for-profit organizations, especially when it comes to public service values? Understanding why individuals engage in public service is arguably more important than ever as social capital and civic engagement decline. This article draws upon the “other-oriented” aspect of public service and builds upon the work of Brewer (Brewer, Gene A. 2003. Building social capital: Civic attitudes and behavior of public servants. Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory 13 (1):5–26.) and Houston (Houston, David J. 2006. “Walking the walk” of public service motivation: Public employees and charitable gifts of time, blood, and money. Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory 16 (1):67–86.; Houston, David J. 2008. Behavior in the public square. In Motivation in public management: The call of public service, eds. James L. Perry and Annie Hondeghem, 177–99. Oxford, UK: Oxford Univ. Press.) to examine the impact of sector on one area of prosocial behavior: volunteering. This article employs data from the September Volunteer Supplement of the 2011 Current Population Survey to examine how both formal and informal volunteering varies across sectors—public, nonprofit, and for-profit—as well as across levels of government—federal, state, and local. This study finds that government and nonprofit sector employees tend to volunteer more than their for-profit sector counterparts, but there are important nuances when taking work schedule, levels of government, and additional measures of volunteering into account.

t: Public Management, Context, and Performance: In Quest of a More General Theory
abs: Recent years have seen a substantial growth in the large-N quantitative study of public management and performance. Much of the progress can be attributed to a small number of data sets on local governments in a few countries. The range of data sets suggests the validity of the overall hypothesis of management affecting performance, but the precise findings also vary across these and other contexts. These various and sometimes conflicting findings suggest that additional gains might be made through developing a theory of context and how context affects the management-performance linkage. This article seeks to take some initial steps in providing such a theory by incorporating such contextual variables as political context (unitary versus shared powers, single- or multiple-level, corporatist versus adversarial, with or without a formal performance appraisal system), environmental context (extent of complexity, turbulence, and also munificence; presence versus absence of social capital), and internal context (extent of goal clarity and consistency, organizational centralization versus decentralization, and degree of professionalism). The theory presents context as a set of variables that condition the impact of management in an interactive model. The theory seeks to unify the existing findings and present a series of hypotheses for further empirical testing.

Social and Task Interdependencies in the Street-Level Implementation of Innovation
abs: Organizations often adopt, though do not always successfully implement, innovations that require widespread frontline participation to realize their full benefits. To better understand the mechanisms that support or inhibit the implementation of such innovations, we apply constructs from organizational learning theory to the case of implementing innovation in schools, and operationalize those constructs in a computational, agent-based model. Model analysis reveals how the misalignment between an organization’s social network and the task structure of its target innovation can impede frontline implementation, even when the individuals inside the organization have the skill and willingness to implement the innovation’s constituent activities. We find that individual-level improvement before the decision to adopt the innovation can exacerbate this problem by reducing the utilization of tasks needed to support future implementation. We translate our insights into specific propositions about how the work required by the target innovation and an organization’s social network relate to the level of frontline implementation in organizations.

t: Representative Bureaucracy in Policing: Does It Increase Perceived Legitimacy?
abs: Drawing on the theory of representative bureaucracy, specifically the theory of symbolic representation, we examine whether or not gender representativeness in a police department’s domestic violence unit influences how citizens judge the agency’s performance, trustworthiness, and fairness. To examine this question, we use an online survey experiment in which we vary the representation of female police officers in a hypothetical domestic violence unit as well as the agency’s performance. Results suggest that gender representation does indeed influence the perceived job performance, trustworthiness, and fairness of the agency, as does the agency’s performance. Thus, this study suggests that the symbolic representativeness of the police does causally influence how citizens view and judge a law enforcement agency, and thus in turn perhaps their willingness to cooperate in the coproduction of public safety outcomes.

t: New Leaders' Managerial Background and the Performance of Public Organizations: The Theory of Publicness Fit
abs: We develop a theory of the effect of top management succession on the performance of public organizations. The theory is rooted in the fundamental characteristics of an organization’s publicness: ownership, funding, and regulation. We construct the concept of publicness fit—the match between the organization and the leader’s previous managerial experience. We argue that the effect of publicness fit on performance depends on the balance of adaptation benefits and disruption costs, which in turn depends on the prior performance of an organization. We propose a research agenda to empirically evaluate propositions developed from the theory of publicness fit.

t: Administrative Burden: Learning, Psychological, and Compliance Costs in Citizen-State Interactions
abs: This article offers two theoretical contributions. First, we develop the concept of administrative burden as an important variable in understanding how citizens experience the state. Administrative burden is conceptualized as a function of learning, psychological, and compliance costs that citizens experience in their interactions with government. Second, we argue that administrative burden is a venue of politics, that is, the level of administrative burden placed on an individual, as well as the distribution of burden between the state and the individual, will often be a function of deliberate political choice rather than simply a product of historical accident or neglect. The opaque nature of administrative burdens may facilitate their use as forms of “hidden politics,” where significant policy changes occur without broad political consideration. We illustrate this argument via an analysis of the evolution of Medicaid policies in the state of Wisconsin. Across three Governorships, the level of burden evolved in ways consistent with the differing political philosophies of each Governor, with federal actors playing a secondary but important role in shaping burden in this intergovernmental program. We conclude by sketching a research agenda centered on administrative burden.

t: Participant Voice in the Bureaucratic Policymaking Process
abs: I examine whether citizens who participate in agency rulemaking in the United States believe they have a meaningful voice. Using data drawn from 388 individuals, I employ an innovative survey research design approach—anchoring vignettes—to measure political efficacy during rulemaking, as well as a randomized survey experiment to study causal drivers. Despite powerful arguments associated with low efficacy, participants report, on average, “a lot of say” during rulemaking. However, experimental evidence suggests that participants believe agencies are more responsive to business interests than to those of ordinary citizens. When taken together, these results imply notable efficacy among those who participate. However, this normatively optimistic finding is tempered by the normatively pessimistic perception that business interests hold a clear advantage over the general public in influencing agency policy decisions.

t: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty with Multiple Exit Options: Evidence from the US Federal Workforce
abs: We assess the turnover intentions of federal employees using Hirschman’s theory of exit, voice, and loyalty. Specifically, we follow other studies that have tested the effects of loyalty and voice on the likelihood a person states their intention to leave. However, using large-scale survey evidence from the federal workforce, we are able to assess the impact of loyalty, voice, and other factors (including assessments of pay) on the likelihood that a respondent will retire, leave for another federal agency, or leave for another sector. Our statistical analysis provides evidence that perceptions about voice and loyalty limit exit. Yet, the effects of voice, loyalty, and pay vary with exit option.

t: The “Guarding the Guardians” Problem: An Analysis of the Organizational Performance of an Internal Affairs Division
abs: Public administration scholars have proposed that efficient monitoring and accountability are key performance elements in public services. We contribute to this debate by focusing on the so-called “guarding the guardians” dilemma: monitoring commissions made up of public officials who may refrain from punishing their peers and turn a blind eye to certain deviations. In the police, this is the case of internal affairs divisions (IADs), which are organizations crafted to monitor the behavior of police officers. We expand the existing literature by proposing a set of hypotheses that are tested using a distinct data set containing detailed information on investigations against police officers performed by an IAD. We assess the organizational performance of the IAD by examining how various factors influence competing hazards of acquittal, mild and harsh punishment of the implicated officers. We find that high-ranking, high-tenured officers are less harshly punished with termination of duty, whereas the opposite effect is found with respect to cases with extensive media coverage. We also find that cases judged by specialized investigation officers increase the likelihood of punishment compared to cases assigned to temporary, rotating commissions, especially for cases with a long time span.

t: The Multiple Levels of Disaster Research
abs: Emotional Labor and Crisis Response, by Sharon Mastracci, Mary Guy, and Meredith Newman, explores jobs that require workers to suppress, engage, exaggerate, and manipulate their own and others’ feelings in order to work more effectively. In disasters, public administrators from the highest policy levels to the first responders must do this in a variety of ways. Success in their jobs requires emotional labor. The authors explore this concept of emotional labor theoretically, frame it within the public administration field, then detail human capital issues, competence and trust, responsibility and accountability, legitimacy and representativeness, and professional standards and discretion in subsequent chapters. Full of incredibly vivid examples, this compelling book employs a useful and often overlooked microlens on this difficult component of public service. Disaster Policy and Politics by Richard Sylves is a well-organized and thorough textbook that explores disaster response from a more macro perspective. It provides an overview of US disaster administration from a variety of public administration, policy, and managerial perspectives. Sylves then specifically highlights the role of the President in disaster declarations, the role of scientists and engineers, the critical role of intergovernmental relations, and civilian-military relationships in chapters laid out nicely, with plenty of short case studies that highlight the topics addressed. Dealing with Disaster by Saundra Schneider is based on case studies and provides a helpful analytical framework, which describes government responses to disasters as a struggle between individual action and institutional or bureaucratic constraints. In developing this framework, Schneider presents the US disaster system and disasters in general as public policy, both in a similar style and manner as Sylves. But Schneider then focuses on human behavior in and around disasters, norms and culture that mitigate and promote success and, finally, the bureaucratic infrastructure of disaster. Part two of Schneider’s book presents eight disasters as cases, each addressing the topics above. These thoughtfully written cases include Hurricanes Hugo, Andrew, Georges and Katrina, the Loma Prieta and Northridge Earthquakes, and the 1990 and 2010 Floods in South Carolina and Tennessee, respectively. Although every case doesn’t follow the analytical framework exactly, they are presented in a very similar fashion, which is helpful for comparative purposes. These three books combined help make sense of the complexity of disasters from rather different perspectives. The more structural view was presented by Sylves. Sylves maps the organizational terrain of disasters, introducing stakeholders and exploring policy implications for each, detailing the political and bureaucratic processes, and identifying the key actors and their roles. The three themes covered, as summarized by the author, are public policy analysis, organizational management, and leadership. The first two are done well, the third to a lesser extent, but still of value. Disaster Policy and Politics serves as an ideal primer on US disaster response, emergency management, and security for students at any level. Perhaps at the other end of the spectrum, Mastracci, Guy, and Newman present a much more focused study on human behavior. Mastracci and colleagues’ work is framed within the disaster complexity discussed by Sylves. This work on emotional labor and crisis response is not their first effort, building upon well-regarded prior work. Emotional Labor and Crisis Response focuses on the first responders themselves. The emotional stresses and skills first responders face are astounding and how they rationalize them even more so. Mastracci, Guy, and Newman document this with riveting first-hand accounts by a wide variety of frontline workers. Schneider’s work represents a middle ground between the other two books. Her cases explore both the macro context as well as the more micro understanding of human behavior, though not at the level of detail evident in Emotional Labor. However, by framing the cases at the organizational level, Schneider bridges the micro and macro with the effective framework presented in the first section of the book. None of the three books spend much time defining disasters or crises. Although this may make the books more accessible and perhaps more widely applicable, it represents a gap to be filled. Sylves’ coverage of disaster declarations comes closest to providing a definition. And Schneider’s cases, though presented without a clear definition of disaster, are understood by the reader to be disasters. However, with Schneider’s framework and the emotional labor theoretical perspective of Mastracci, Guy, and Newman, I found myself wondering about the applicability of these works across various types and intensities of disaster. Clearly 9/11 transformed the institutional scaffolding established to address disasters in the United States. How was this event more than a disaster? Are natural disasters theoretically different than terrorist attacks? And if so, how? With respect to the institutional and organizational response, perhaps yes. What about at the level of individual or bureaucratic response? The frameworks presented by both Schneider and Mastracci, Guy, and Newman, seem useful regardless of disaster type. Schneider discussed this in her selection of different types of disasters. The disasters she covered are different types (hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes), but all are natural. The variance in her coverage was largely based on public perception of effective action regarding each case. In pursuit of disaster theory, however, what about global warming, famine, large scale food poisoning or product tampering? These different types of disasters would certainly differ in terms of agencies involved, but perhaps to a lesser degree regarding individual action and bureaucratic response. Moreover, how might less devastating “organizational disasters” fit into this body of work? Focusing the microlens of analysis on the frontline, and even more clearly on emotional labor, reveals insights likely applicable to many types of workers in situations that may not always be as extreme as the cases discussed by Mastracci, Guy, and Newman or Schneider. One of the problems with disaster research is the choice of unit of analysis and observation for analyzing disasters. The three books make different decisions in this regard. Bringing these different perspectives together would be useful in developing a theoretical framework that spans the macro policy environment, the organizational level, and individual implementation to conceptualize disasters and crises. One might consider the degree to which stakeholder worldviews are challenged at each of these levels as an indicator of the impact of a particular disaster. We might consider high reliability organizations (HROs) that fend off disaster or the negative outcomes of disaster. What are the limits of HROs regarding size and scope of potential disasters? Disasters impact stakeholders differently. Some strike all equally, crippling government with institutional voids, even if only temporary. Others are far more selective; consider a technological problem, such as a massive cyber attack, for example. A framework with the capacity to address such questions could move disaster research forward conceptually—beyond an external stimulus to an organization. These three books offer hints for developing such a framework. Let me now explore each book in turn. Sylves presents a textbook; detailed, logical, and linear. The first chapter provides readers with an overview of disaster management from historical, bureaucratic, political, and technical perspectives. The second chapter frames disaster management within the social sciences. This is the least well-developed aspect of the book. The stress is on professionalization of responders, but the contrast between Jeffersonian and Hamiltonian public managers seems overdone and the attention given to organizational, economic, and other public administration models is lacking. A stakeholder or institutional lens would have sufficed to house all of the snapshots provided. If used in a class, this chapter might provide a useful start, but would require some framing within the public administration literature to navigate the topics discussed. The next few chapters make up for this minor weakness. Sylves’s coverage of the evolution of emergency management from the Cold War and the Civil Defense Act of 1950, through the Disaster Relief Act of 1974, FEMA in 1979, and the War on Terror and Homeland Security is well done and indeed sets the stage for a broad understanding of federal emergency management. Chapter Three, Historical Trends in Disaster Management, would make a good reading for a section on disaster response in a more traditional public administration and policy class. Chapter Four provides a more specific analysis of the role of the presidency in declaring disasters. Although this might seem a bit of a niche topic within a broad text like this, its importance emerges with a reread of the previous chapter. Much can be learned about presidential responses to global and national threats and disasters and their institutionalization into our public administration. The Presidential Disaster Declaration table in the “how it works” textbox is one of a number of tables and flowcharts that make sense of intergovernmental affairs and federalism in the otherwise chaotic and seemingly unorganized context of disaster response. The Role of Scientists and Engineers is an interesting chapter but raises the question of why many other stakeholders are not included. The Intergovernmental Relations and Civil-Military Relations chapters (6 and 7) are both valuable. They map out the complexity of disasters and emergency management—going further with Chapter 8 on the Globalization of Disasters to describe very briefly the international arena of large scale emergency management. The concluding chapter summarizes each previous chapter. Disaster Policy and Politics would make an excellent text for a section on disasters or emergency management at multiple levels, undergraduate and graduate. I found the historical overviews, flowcharts, and reporting arrangement very helpful. The many mini-cases, “how things work,” and “history’s lessons” will be useful for generating class discussion. The Sylves’ text does not, however, go into great depth (with the exception perhaps of the role of the presidency in disasters) on any one dimension or particular case. For this, explore the Schneider book. Schneider’s work is ideally suited to be read in conjunction with the Sylves’ text. The first part of the book explores disasters as a public policy issue in great theoretical depth. Schneider’s brief history of governmental disaster assistance policy nicely complements Sylves’ book. It is perhaps more academic in appearance with heavy use of citations, where Sylves’ work is more explanatory. Regardless, the review of history and the chapter on the governmental response system are very well done. Then the book accelerates. The fourth chapter presents two sets of norms—one anchored in human behavior, and the second in governmental activity and more specifically bureaucracy. Focusing on topics such as “unanticipated events,” “milling,” “rumors,” and “keynoting” demonstrates the ground level perspective Schneider brings to this work. This is smart analysis that could have been expanded and framed more thoroughly to present the building blocks of a theory of disaster management. Regardless, this first part of the book does a wonderful job grounding the reader before presenting the cases. In part two, Schneider presents the eight cases—all major disasters that vary in terms of public perception of effectiveness. The cases also cover different time periods, with distinct bureaucratic and political realities that could be explored more systematically. Some of the cases are presented in more depth than others. And I would have preferred that all of the well-grounded theoretical insights were addressed in each case (milling, rumors, keynoting, etc.). Instead, only the most relevant or important variables were highlighted in each case. But, they are presented in a similar fashion with similar headings which does help in the invariable cross-checking required to compare responses and insights. Dealing with Disaster: Public Management in Crisis Situations is a more scholarly text than Sylves’ descriptive work and would make a solid companion reader to that more generic text. The theoretical framing at the onset would make this useful in a course on disasters, a section on disasters in a public management, policy or administration course, or a management or organization theory course (strategy, stakeholders) seeking disaster response as a unique case to expose more fundamental issues about individual behaviors and bureaucratic responses to crisis. For more depth here, I turn to the third book in this review. The Mastracci, Guy, and Newman book starts with the human behavior dimension presented by Schneider, and then goes into incredible depth to build a complex but well-grounded understanding of the emotional labor of first responders and crisis workers. Their scholarly qualitative approach with first-hand stories and exceedingly personal tales brings the reader into the hearts and minds of these frontline workers. Moreover, Mastracci et al. are pushing a theoretical agenda that is already well established in their previous work. Of course, doing so suggests this book is the most specific and niched of the three. However, it is not outside of the grasp of undergraduates. The first-hand accounts are so compelling that they alone will elicit student conversation where the more complex interpretations of those events might take some explaining. Regardless, this work is impressive and moving. The book begins by detailing and defining emotional labor—managing one’s own or another’s feelings to get a job done. This work will remind readers of Hochschild’s Managed Heart repackaged for a public administration audience and then, a most interesting one, where workers perform on the razor’s edge. Mastracci et al. stress repeatedly that emotional labor is not emotional intelligence, it is not public service motivation, it is not leadership—and yet the stories informants tell have incredible bearing on all three of those important areas of study—as well as emotional labor. Moreover, the grounded research reveals coping strategies and best practices in such intimate detail that they could only have come from workers in the field; “psychological first aid,” putting intense images into “little closets in my mind”; the “crazy calm” of focus in situations where all others see blood, death and chaos; and common sense and humor. Although the authors go out of their way to stress that emotional labor is not public service motivation or leadership or emotional intelligence, all three are required and all three are clearly related to emotional labor in these extreme settings. The subsequent chapters discuss in incredible detail the strategies responders use to manage emotions, coping strategies, and self-care plans, as well as traits they seek when hiring others and warning signs when supervising stressed employees. The authors employ the technique of long participant narratives. This can be excruciating in some qualitative studies. Not here. Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this work is that their respondents understand this concept of emotional labor and discuss it in great depth. Emotional labor is present in their preparation, response, and recovery before, during, and after crisis. The next several chapters detail, through respondents’ voices, the components of emotional labor that must be managed, like communicating competence and cultivating trust (Chapter 4). Imagine the public information officer providing details of a horrendous act or the difficulty in managing the media on such sensitive issues. As I read this chapter I recalled the Newtown, Connecticut police officer making the initial statements to the press about what happened that tragic day. What in that man’s experience could have possibly prepared him for that moment? These chapters detail how public servants manage such activities and how they internalize the decisions they make. Chapter 5 highlights government responsiveness and accountability to departments, to jobs, to citizens, and to humanity. For example, a police lieutenant suggested a great deal of his job is acting, improvising, and weighing different responses. Hearing an officer suggest a “great deal” of his job is “acting” might disturb some, but framed within this book one cannot help but wonder when these first responders are not acting. They also stress professional standards and discretion (Chapter 7) that help some first responders cope and help others help clients choose different paths. Consider the statement from an officer saying that normally or in the past he would have “blindly followed the law. Not tonight, sweetheart. No way.” This officer had seen enough cases to know something was amiss. But an officer saying he was not going to follow the law? How do we train for that? How do we give those working on the frontline discretion and power to make the “right” decisions at times of extreme stress? Such questions cut to the core of public administration theory. Emotional Labor and Crisis Response helps us make sense of such difficult questions that strike at the heart of public administration and “publicness.” The chapter on legitimacy, representativeness, and gender (Chapter 6) addresses those questions to some degree, but only scratches the surface. These actors rely on their casting and learn to do well with what they have; perhaps playing roles that will make those in the crisis more comfortable or likely to be of assistance. This is a fascinating book that can indeed be used at the undergraduate level because of the accessible narratives. However, its real value would be in courses or sections on public service motivation, leadership, and emotional intelligence, despite the authors’ worries that it could be confused with those topics. t: Leadership and Performance of Public Employees: Effects of the Quality and Characteristics of Manager-Employee Relationships
abs: Few studies in public management have assessed whether managerial leadership has any influence on job performance of public employees. This study employs a well-established theory of leadership, leader-member exchange (LMX) theory, to consider the effects of the manager-employee relationship on ratings of employee in-role and extra-role performance. It also investigates how differences in gender between the manager and employee and duration of their relationship may influence the effects of LMX on employee job performance. We examine these linkages with data from two surveys of 477 employees and 161 managers working in a large state government agency. We find that when the quality of LMX is high, employees receive higher performance ratings, and this association is moderated by difference in gender between an employee and manager and the duration of time an employee has worked for a particular manager. We discuss implications of our findings and avenues for future research for public management scholarship. We also offer suggestions for public management practice regarding how to develop high-quality relationships with employees. O propósito deste artigo é apresentar ideias sobre as condições nas quais empregados do governo são mais propensos a se engajarem em ações para melhorar o desempenho de suas organizações. Neste esforço, a pesquisa examina os efeitos diretos e interativos da liderança ética e das percepções do controle pessoal em comportamentos centrados em melhorias entre os empregados do governo. Estes relacionamentos foram examinados com dados que coletados através de dois levantamentos isolados com 477 empregados e 161 gerentes que trabalham em uma agência estadual de grande porte. Os resultados indicam que a liderança ética e o controle pessoal, depois de controladas por características pessoais dos empregados, satisfação no trabalho, procedimentos de equidade e monitoramento do desempenho, são positivamente relacionados com as avaliações que os subordinados fazem sobre os supervisores que lidam com comportamentos de expressão. Os resultados também demonstram que os efeitos da liderança ética no comportamento de expressão tornam-se significativamente mais fortes quando os empregados percebem que eles possuem níveis maiores de discernimento sobre o comportamento no trabalho e influência nas decisões em seus grupos. Assim, as implicações destas descobertas para a prática e para a pesquisa são discutidas. Translated by Ricardo Gomes, University of Brasília

t: Interorganizational Engagement in Collaborative Environmental Management: Evidence from the South Florida Ecosystem Restoration Task Force
abs: Collaboration is commonly used to deliver public services that reach beyond the individual capacities of independent organizations. Although much of the literature in the fields of collaborative governance has offered theoretical insights to explain how stakeholders might initially enter into collaborative processes or how the design of collaborative processes can support continued stakeholder participation over time, the literature has not effectively studied what factors might drive actors to engage one another in a particular conversation or discussion during a collaborative process, nor what factors affect whether engagement is cooperative or conflictual. We fill this gap through a more “micro-level” view of collaborative engagement in a study of the South Florida Ecosystem Restoration Task Force, a collaborative arrangement involving representatives from 14 federal, tribal, state, and local agencies, charged with advising and coordinating the efforts in South Florida to restore and recover the Florida Everglades. We use data from coded meeting minutes of discussions among the participants in the South Florida Ecosystem Restoration Program Task Force over a 5-year time frame and demonstrate that the types of issues under discussion and the actors involved in discussion can either foster or inhibit engagement and conflict during dialogue. Our results have important implications for the development of a stronger theory of collaborative engagement in interorganizational partnerships.

t: How Does Public Service Motivation Among Teachers Affect Student Performance in Schools?
abs: The literature expects public service motivation (PSM) to affect performance, but most of the existing studies of this relationship use subjective performance data and focus on output rather than outcome. This article investigates the association between PSM and the performance of Danish teachers using an objective outcome measure (the students' academic performance in their final examinations). Combining survey data and administrative register data in a multilevel data set, we are able to control very robustly for the specific characteristics of the students (n = 5,631), the schools (n = 85), and other teacher characteristics (n = 694) besides PSM. We find that PSM is positively associated with examination marks. The result indicates that PSM may be relevant for performance improvements.

t: Opportunism and Honest Incompetence—Seeking Explanations for Noncompliance in Public Procurement
abs: This article utilizes agency theory to explain maverick buying in governmental agencies, that is, noncompliance to centrally negotiated frame agreements. Traditional agency theory assumes the agent to be an opportunistic self-interest seeker. A complementary view of agency problems portrays man as an honest, yet not fully competent, actor; both agents and principals may be burdened by “honest incompetence.” We apply both perspectives on principal-agent relationships to study maverick buying in government procurement and link agency problems to three governance mechanisms: monitoring, training, and guidance. We find that guidance and training help to reduce governmental employees’ noncompliance, but output monitoring does not. Our findings further indicate that maverick buying is related to goal incongruence and two different types of information asymmetry: Agency problems may arise not only because the agent has information the principal is not aware of but also because the principal may have information the agent is not aware of. Future research in public management using agency theory to study instances of hidden action could benefit from applying a similar dual lens to behaviors previously examined as purely opportunistic.

t: Determinants of Charter County Decisions: An Event History Analysis of Florida Counties
abs: The establishment of a county charter, or “home-rule” provision, is intended to remove the resolution of local problems from the state legislature’s busy agenda and give the county greater control over its regional affairs. Although the literature has paid significant attention to the institutional determinants of local city structure and reform, little is understood about how and why a county would reform its governing system. For example, not all counties able to adopt a charter do so, nor are all adoption attempts successful. Using an event history analysis approach and data of Florida counties from 1973 through 2008, we draw on the theory of constitutional contracts to determine the demographic, economic, and political determinants of charter adoption.

t: Boundaries as Junctures: Collaborative Boundary Work for Building Efficient Resilience
abs: This article is a theoretical contribution to reconsidering the boundaries that are central features of collaborative public management. We identify two contrasting ways of doing boundary work: one oriented to treating them as barriers that promote separation and the other to treating them as junctures that enable connecting. We describe three general practices for creating junctures: translating across, aligning among, and decentering differences. We argue that orienting boundary work in collaboration to making connections supports efficient resilience, making it possible for systems to work even when they are disrupted or when resources are constrained. We illustrate the practices and their benefits with examples from collaborative public management.

t: Strengthening Contract Management Capacity to Ensure Accountability
abs: In The Responsible Contract Manager: Protecting the Public Interest in an Outsourced World, Steven Cohen and William Eimicke excelled at a difficult task; through careful analysis and insights, they crafted a book relevant for both public management scholars and practitioners alike. The authors unpack the important work of contract managers, seeking to improve decision making throughout the contracting lifecycle while at the same time protecting public interest and maintaining accountability. The text provides a balanced discussion of the pros and cons of public sector contracting, focusing on contracting as a tool, not approaching it from an entrenched ideological position. In fact, the book is remarkably devoid of ideological and normative wrangling that often polarizes audiences on the topic of government contracting. Cohen and Eimicke fairly assert that while ideology can lead to poor contracting decisions, it can also be a stumbling block to furthering the relevant and timely advancement of contract management work and research. They argue that, in order for contracting to be successful—beyond just meeting efficiency goals—the tool must also “…be understood and adapted to conform to the requirements of representative democracy” (20). The perils of organizational inattention to contract management are profoundly consequential—poor management leads to corruption, programmatic failure, and compromised institutions. The book is subdivided into five sections, but these can be distilled into two distinct components. The first, which is most relevant to public management scholars, captures issues of ethics, representative democracy, and accountability. The second part of the book turns toward the practical, focusing on the make-or-buy decision, contractor selection, the complexities of contract management, performance measurement and management, and poignant case studies in contracting success and failure. It is this holistic treatment of contracting and contract management that makes The Responsible Contract Manager equally pertinent to students, practitioners, and academic scholars. In the first chapter, Cohen and Eimicke define the government contract, in clear principal-agent terms, as a formal relationship with private execution but public control, funding, and decision-making authority. The authors examine existing scholarship and current contracting trends to establish a baseline of knowledge of government contracting. Chapter 3 captures the latest developments in network theory and the increasing practical imperative and political preference for work through multilayered network structures involving government, private, and nonprofit actors. Cohen and Eimicke could have used this chapter as a follow-up to chapter 1 and focused on the spectrum of privatization activities rather than exclusively networks. A derivative of what Salamon (2002) and Hodge (2000) present in their works on the topic would benefit the reader (particularly students and practitioners) and put the networks discussion in better context. The conceptual core emerges in chapters 2 and 4 as the authors delve into issues of contracting ethics, representative democracy, and accountability—all of which are relevant to public management scholars analyzing the design and governance of American institutions. Chapter 2 focuses on the ethical dimensions of contracting and contract management. The heart of Cohen and Eimicke’s position is that fundamental goal divergence occurs between the contract manager and the private contractor. In all probability these two cultures will influence each other and possibly clash. The private firm may adopt some of the mission-driven characteristics and risk-averse behavior of government organizations; the government officials might start focusing on the size of their paychecks and the wealth created by the programs they manage (25). This opportunity for discord clearly poses a management challenge, but more troubling is the opportunity for abuse and corruption, which the authors tackle in the next part of the chapter. Cohen and Eimicke demonstrate that corruption associated with contracting poses a serious threat to public interest. The authors catalog the sources of corruption in the contract process, to include bribes, kickbacks, revolving door employment, political contributions, and incompetence. The latter, incompetence, is perhaps the most understudied and undervalued form of ethical breach. I assert this is no subtle point given the rise in contracting and implications for contract managers (e.g., distribution of workload, complexity of contracts, level of training, etc.). To illustrate, the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) has no shortage of studies on the need to address the performance of the federal acquisition workforce, citing skills gaps, personnel shortages, and hiring reforms, among other systemic personnel issues that affect contracting outcomes (see US GAO 2013, 2012). Cohen and Eimicke conclude chapter 2 by explaining the ways in which our current system seeks to stymie corruption to include prevention (legal and process-oriented mechanisms), monitoring, and procedures aimed explicitly to mitigate corrupt practices. Yet they also suggest additional techniques to curb corruption—stronger and more specified laws aimed at preventing unethical behavior by contractors and public managers and skills-based training to mitigate managerial incompetence. Chapter 4 presents a robust historical narrative of democratic representation and accountability. The chapter serves as a conceptual anchor to the broader narrative on public values put forth in the book, relevant for public management scholars, but of particular interest to practitioners who might be discovering this perspective for the first time. Cohen and Eimicke peel away the layers of accountability to address the institutions and connections between citizens and their government. In doing so, they trace the intellectual and political history of democratic representation, starting with the Hobbesian conception of the social contract; that is, delegated authority to the sovereign to represent the individual captured as representation as authority. The belief that the represented hold power is reflected in their discussion of representation as accountability whereby some measure of authority remains with the represented to ensure the representative is responsive. The principles of representative democracy—representatives have attitudes, beliefs, and attributes reflective of the represented—are understood as descriptive representation. The symbols of the power between the represented government and the represented (e.g., flag) are described as symbolic representation. Finally, representation as responsible stewardship is captured in the belief that good stewardship is ensured through representative government. It is through this final lens that Cohen and Eimicke operationalize representation throughout the text. With this mind, contractors have a role in the process as a responsible steward. Accountability is far more than simply doing what their [contractors] contracts specify. Accountability requires that contractors act as the agents of a representative system where the directions they receive are designed to both respond to public views and ensure that government functions effectively (86). The authors stress that as we extend the accountability chain from citizen to elected representative to unelected bureaucrat to private contractor, the government has a responsibility to ensure the deeply rooted value of representation is reflected in our contract management practices. Next, Cohen and Eimicke shift their focus toward bureaucratic policymaking, tracing the source of bureaucratic power via expertise and information to the implementation process, namely through discretionary decision making. The authors examine the linkage between citizen and the unelected bureaucracy and the position and rights of contractors from varying external and internal institutions including the judiciary and legislature. Through this exercise, Cohen and Eimicke show that contracting increases the complexities and difficulties of maintaining accountability in government. Furthermore, contractor behavior is less constrained than bureaucratic behavior, a worrisome development. The authors argue that bureaucrats should not only have control over contractor behavior, but that contractors should act in “…the spirit of the contract as well as the letter of the contract” (86) to achieve accountability. Fostering this multidimensional perspective of democratic representation and charging public managers to apply it to the contracting context is among the greatest contributions of the book. The remaining chapters focus on the practical elements of contract management, particularly relevant for practitioner readers. In chapter 5, Cohen and Eimicke address the make-or-buy decision, focusing on what matters when assessing whether to contract. The authors discuss government management capacity, contractor capacity, core and noncore functions (and they are careful to point out these can change over time), and chain of command and accountability as dimensions to consider when making the decision to outsource. The authors interestingly refer to the decision to contract not as an “on/off” decision, but rather as a continuum. Two contributions emerge from this understanding. First, maintaining some element of in-house capacity—in terms of both contract management and technical ability to perform outsourced services—can increase government bargaining power and contract accountability. Second, Cohen and Eimicke argue that separating policy formulation (performed by government managers) from policy implementation (performed by contractors) by ensuring that public officials maintain strategic capacity and decision-making authority can also lead to strengthened accountability through better management of contract processes. Chapters 6–8 focus on the contract management process. Chapter 6 provides guidance on selecting the best contractor. The authors then cleverly discuss the work of contract managers after contractor selection in chapter 7 by outlining 20 common problems associated with contract management. The range of problems and ways to address them are vast: flawed contract design, appropriate capture and management of transaction costs, communication, ensure contractor capacity meets needs of the contract, resource issues within the government agency, and political dimensions of contract management. In chapter 8, the authors address performance measurement including the use of contract incentives and other tools available to manage contracts. The authors note that the ongoing challenges to public managers both to understand the right tools to induce performance and to access those tools. Cohen and Eimicke underscore that paramount to these activities is retaining, training, and soliciting contract managers with the appropriate skills to carry out this and other management functions. The authors then present contracting case studies in chapters 9–11. Cohen and Eimicke use examples from federal and local agencies to show (a) when not to contract—that is internally “make” and not “buy” the good or service in question; (b) when contracting works; and (c) when contracting does not work. Through the cases, the authors are careful to designate the ups, downs, and corrective actions along the way to ensure success. Success is ultimately dependent on contract design and management, and more often it is specifically observed through performance-based contracting and well-crafted performance outcomes. These cases are especially beneficial for instructors in search of contracting cases to use in the classroom. This application, if used in conjunction with the preceding chapters, would help students to understand practical application of the principles and guidance prescribed by the authors. Cohen and Eimicke assert in their concluding chapter (which is teed up in chapters 6 and 7) that management capacity is critical to upholding the values of representative democracy and accountability. But it’s the right kind of capacity that matters. Contract management requires special skills, which are more comprehensive than requisite internal management skills. Contract managers must have an understanding of the contracted work, be able to design an effective solicitation and selection criteria, monitor the work, communicate with the contractor, develop, maintain and evaluate performance measures and incentives, and have the ability to use good judgment in measuring contract outcomes. Cohen and Eimicke demonstrate that fundamental change in the public sector contract management workforce is required to meet the needs of the expanded contracting environment while maintaining accountability. Furthermore, it is dangerous to shed capacity required to administer contracts and provide strategic management of the organization’s service delivery portfolio. This provides an area for further empirical research. Privatization scholars have focused on the importance of government capacity, but little attention has been paid to the appropriateness or mix of skills that are required in this changing landscape. Simply maintaining or adding public employees, without consideration of assembling the right skill sets, will not solve the contract management capacity problem that currently exists in many public organizations. The Responsible Contract Manager is a must read for public management scholars and contract managers. For practitioners, this book will serve to remind them of the important task they are undertaking—upholding the public interest—as they deliver public services through contracts. Public management scholars can instructively use the book in the classroom to underscore the significance of public values in contract management and the crucial decisions public managers make when managing contracts. Through case discussion, instructors can move students through the contract lifecycle, beginning with the make-or-buy decision, to analyze the decision-making calculus at each phase. Scholars should also note the relevance of the content to our field and our obligation to be attentive to public values in our implementation structures.
